title: Nine Out of Ten
excerpt: Of every 100 children born in Liberia, only 10 will ever finish primary school. The number is shocking, but the reasons behind it are the more important story.
body:
Of every 100 children born in Liberia, only 10 will ever finish primary school. The number is shocking on its own. But the reasons behind it — and the path out — are the story we want to tell.

We've been asked, more than once, whether that statistic is real. It is. The figure comes from the official Annual School Census published by Liberia's Ministry of Education for 2021–22. It is the same source international donors and the World Bank rely on. And it is consistent with everything else we see in Liberia.

A country of children

Liberia's population is roughly 5.18 million. More than 40% of those people are of school-going age. Liberia is, demographically, a country of children. That share is not shrinking. It is expected to keep growing for the rest of this century.

This is the first thing to understand. The story of Liberian education is not a story about a small underserved minority. It is a story about a generation that includes a meaningful fraction of the entire country.

The funnel of attrition

Here is what happens to those children, level by level, according to the most recent census:

  • Only 46% of primary-school-aged children are enrolled in primary school. More than half of Liberia's youngest learners are missing from a classroom they should be in.
  • Only 21% of junior-secondary-aged children are enrolled in junior secondary. Four out of every five middle-school-aged children are not in middle school.
  • Only 17% of senior-secondary-aged children are enrolled in senior secondary. More than eight in ten high-school-aged kids are not in high school.
  • Only 10% of children ever finish even primary school.

Those numbers describe a system that is losing children at every gate.

The classroom they walk into

For the children who do make it inside, the conditions are not what most readers will recognize as a school.

In a Liberian high school, 32 students share a single math textbook. In some senior schools, that number reaches 65.

Only 8% of all schools in Liberia have piped drinking water. More than half rely on hand pumps. Some children still drink from creeks.

109 schools in Liberia can only be reached by canoe.

These are not edge cases. They are averages and counts from the national census.

Even when Liberian children make it to a classroom, the basics aren't there.

The economic reality

The reason most children are not in school is not a mystery. The average daily income in Liberia is $2.04 per person (World Bank, 2022). Tuition for a single school term, plus a uniform and a bag of textbooks, costs roughly what a typical family earns in two months.

Three crises within a single generation — civil war from 1989 to 2003, the Ebola outbreak from 2014 to 2016, and COVID from 2020 onward — closed schools for years at a time and pushed families into deeper poverty. When daily survival is the priority, school fees become an impossible luxury.

This is the part that does not show up in a single statistic. The 10% completion rate is not a story about children who chose to leave. It is a story about families forced to make the same hard choice, hundreds of thousands of times.

What we are doing about it

CECE's Dream is not trying to solve the entire system. We do one thing: we cover the cost of school for individual children, one at a time. Tuition, uniform, books, and a monthly check-in to make sure they are still showing up and learning.

A $30/month sponsorship covers the full cost of a Liberian student's school year. The system will not fix itself for the 10%. But it does not have to. The buildings are already standing. The teachers are already there. What's missing — for the average Liberian family — is the affordability of the seat.

Sponsor a student.

Sources

  • Liberia Education Statistics Report 2021-22 — Republic of Liberia Ministry of Education — primary source for enrollment, completion, textbook, water, and access figures
  • GDP per capita (current US$) — World Bank, Liberia — source for the $2.04/day daily income figure
  • Liberia: Trends in Completion Rates by Education Level and Gender — UNESCO IICBA — corroborates the primary completion rate
